3140:
When two (or more) things are complementary, they work together in a way that makes each other better, fuller, or more complete — because each one supplies what the other is missing.

The essential condition is this: the things must be different from each other. Their differences are not a problem — those differences are the reason they pair so well. One covers the gap the other leaves behind.

Think of a lock and a key. They are completely different objects. But that difference is exactly why they work as a pair. Each one completes the other. That is the spirit of "complementary."

"Complementary" always describes a relationship between things, not a property of one thing alone. You cannot say something is complementary on its own. It is always complementary to something else, or complementary with something else.

When things are complementary:

  • Together, they produce something greater, more balanced, or more complete than either could alone.
  • Their strengths and weaknesses offset each other.
  • The whole becomes stronger than the sum of its parts.

Examples in everyday life:

  • "She is creative and spontaneous; he is analytical and methodical. Their personalities are complementary — together, they make a great team."
    She brings what he lacks. He brings what she lacks. Neither is "better." They simply fill each other's gaps.
  • "Cheese and wine are complementary flavours."
    The sharpness of cheese and the acidity of wine offset and enhance each other in a way that neither achieves alone.
  • "His strengths in marketing are complementary to her strengths in product design."
    One knows how to build the product; the other knows how to sell it. Together, they cover the full picture.

Colors

In art and design, complementary colors are pairs of colors that sit directly opposite each other on the color wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. When placed side by side, they make each other appear more vivid and intense. They don't blend into each other — they contrast sharply, and that contrast is what makes them mutually enhancing.

Geometry / Mathematics

Two angles are complementary angles when they add up to exactly 90°. For example, a 30° angle and a 60° angle are complementary — together, they form a right angle (a complete quarter-turn). One "completes" the other to reach that whole.

Medicine and healthcare

You will often see the phrase complementary medicine or complementary therapy — such as acupuncture, yoga, or herbal treatments used alongside standard medical treatment. "Complementary" here means: used in addition to conventional medicine, not instead of it. The two approaches work alongside each other to address different aspects of health.

Music

Two instruments, melodies, or harmonies can be called complementary when they occupy different sonic spaces — one fills in the spaces the other leaves. A bass guitar and a lead guitar are complementary: one lays a low-frequency foundation, the other carries the melody up high. Together, they make a fuller sound.

"Complementary" carries a positive, harmonious tone. It is not just "different" — it is usefully different. It suggests that the pairing is fitting, balanced, and productive. The word implies there is a kind of natural rightness to the combination.
The one mistake almost everyone makes: "complementary" vs. "complimentary"

These two words look nearly identical and are constantly confused, even by native speakers. They mean completely different things.

Complementary (with an e)completing, enhancing, going well together
Complimentary (with an i)(1) expressing praise or admiration, OR (2) given free of charge

Examples of "complimentary" (the other word):

  • "The professor was very complimentary about her essay." → He praised it.
  • "The hotel offers complimentary breakfast." → The breakfast is free.

A simple memory trick: complEment → complEte. The e connects both words. If something completes or fills a gap, use the e spelling. If someone is being nice or something is free, use the i spelling.
Complementary means: two or more different things that, when brought together, complete, balance, or enhance each other — each supplying what the other lacks.
3141:
"Complex" describes something that has many parts, layers, or factors — and crucially, those parts are all connected to and dependent on each other. Because of this interconnectedness, the whole thing is difficult to fully understand, explain, or handle in a quick or simple way.

Think of a spider's web. Each thread connects to many others. Pull one thread, and others shift. That is the essence of complexity: many parts, all woven together.
It's About Structure, Not Just Difficulty

This is what most people miss. "Complex" is not simply a fancy word for "hard" or "difficult." It specifically describes the nature of something — the fact that it has many interrelated pieces.

A locked safe can be hard to open, but it isn't complex — it has a simple mechanism with one purpose. The global economy, on the other hand, is complex — it involves millions of people, businesses, governments, currencies, and supply chains, all constantly affecting each other. You cannot understand one part without understanding how it connects to everything else.

The difficulty in grasping something complex comes from this structure — from the fact that everything is entangled with everything else.

These two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, but when used precisely:

Complicated means difficult. Something complicated has many steps or requires skill, but if you follow the process carefully, you can work through it and reach a clear solution. A complicated math problem, for instance, can be solved reliably once you learn the method.

Complex means made of many interconnected parts, where the parts keep influencing each other, often in unpredictable ways. Even after you understand each individual piece, the whole thing still resists a neat, final understanding. A human relationship is complex — even if you understand both people deeply, their emotions, history, expectations, and moods constantly interact, and there is no formula to "solve" it.

A good way to feel the difference: complicated things can be mastered. Complex things can be understood more deeply over time, but rarely fully mastered.

Things are not simply "complex" or "not complex" — they range from slightly complex to extraordinarily complex.

A bicycle is somewhat complex: gears, brakes, a chain, wheels — all working together. A car is more complex. A jet engine more so. The human brain, with roughly 86 billion neurons all forming trillions of connections, is among the most complex things known to exist.
When People, Emotions, and Situations Are "Complex"

A complex person is someone with many sides, layers, and sometimes contradictions — someone who cannot be easily summed up. They might be warm in some ways and cold in others, hold deep convictions that sometimes seem to conflict, or behave differently depending on context. Understanding them takes time and genuine attention. Calling someone complex is usually not a criticism — it often signals depth and richness of character.

A complex emotion is one that is not pure or clean. Joy mixed with sadness (what you might feel at a loved one's graduation), love entangled with frustration, grief that contains gratitude — these are complex emotions because multiple emotional threads are present at once, sometimes pulling in different directions. They resist simple labels.

A complex situation is one where many factors are at play simultaneously, where there is no single clear cause, no single right answer, and where changing one thing ripples outward and affects many others. Issues like poverty, climate change, or long-running conflicts between nations are classic examples of complex situations.
"Complex" Can Also Signal Richness and Depth

"Complex" is not always used in a frustrated or overwhelmed tone. In many contexts, it carries a positive meaning — indicating depth, sophistication, and richness.

A wine described as complex has many flavors and aromas layered together — fruit, oak, earth, spice — all interacting in ways that reward careful attention. A complex piece of music has many threads of melody, rhythm, and harmony weaving together in ways that reveal more with each listen. A complex character in a novel feels real precisely because they have contradictions, flaws, and depth rather than being flat and predictable.

In these uses, complexity is something to admire rather than dread.

"Complex" pairs naturally with many words you will encounter:

  • a complex problem — one with many causes, no simple fix
  • a complex system — like the immune system, the internet, or a rainforest ecosystem
  • a complex issue — like inequality, addiction, or geopolitical conflict
  • a complex relationship — personal or political, with history and many moving parts
  • a complex character — in fiction, one who feels real, with depth and inner contradictions
  • a complex network — roads, nerves, computers: many nodes all connected
  • a complex process — many stages that interact with each other

The direct opposite of complex is simple. Something simple has few parts, those parts do not depend heavily on each other, and the whole thing is easy to understand at a glance.

A light switch is simple: on or off, one part, one purpose. A smart power grid is complex: millions of devices, real-time data flowing in all directions, automatic adjustments, all interconnected and all affecting each other continuously.

If you remember only one thing: complex = many parts, all connected to each other, making the whole difficult to fully grasp.

The more parts there are, and the more they interact with and influence each other, the more complex something is.
3142: The word complexion has two distinct layers of meaning: one is physical and specific, the other is abstract and general. Both, however, share a common thread — they refer to the overall appearance or character of something, how something looks or feels as a whole.
Meaning 1: The Appearance of a Person's Skin (Especially the Face)

This is the primary and most everyday meaning of the word.

Your complexion is the natural color, tone, texture, and overall visual quality of your skin — especially on your face. When people talk about complexion, they are typically referring to what your skin looks like at a glance: its shade, its clarity, its smoothness, and its general health.

Think of it this way: if someone were to describe your face without focusing on your features (eyes, nose, mouth), they would be describing your complexion. It is the canvas of your face — the background quality of the skin itself.

What complexion includes:

  • Skin tone / color — whether someone's skin is pale, fair, light, medium (sometimes called "wheatish"), olive, tan, brown, dark brown, or deep. This is the most commonly understood aspect of complexion.
  • Clarity and evenness — whether the skin looks smooth and uniform, or has spots, blemishes, redness, dark patches, or uneven areas.
  • Texture and radiance — whether the skin appears glowing and healthy, dull and tired, oily, dry, or rough.

All of these things together make up a person's complexion.

Examples in sentences:

  • "She had a fair complexion with rosy cheeks."
  • "Years of working outdoors gave him a dark, weathered complexion."
  • "The doctor noticed that the patient had a yellowish complexion, which could be a sign of jaundice."
  • "She washed her face every night to maintain a clear complexion."
  • "He had a warm, olive complexion typical of people from that region."

Important nuance: Complexion is not just about color. Two people can have the same skin color but very different complexions — because one person's skin might be smooth and glowing, while the other's is rough and dull. Complexion is the whole picture of how the skin looks and feels.
Meaning 2: The General Character or Nature of Something (Abstract Use)

This is the second, more figurative meaning of complexion. It is used less in casual speech but often appears in journalism, literature, and formal discussion.

Here, complexion refers to the overall nature, character, tone, or aspect of a situation, event, period, or thing — essentially, "what something looks like" in a broader, non-physical sense. It conveys the idea that something has a certain quality, feel, or character that defines it.

Think of it as asking: "What kind of thing is this? What is its general nature or mood?"

Examples in sentences:

  • "The election results changed the entire political complexion of the country."
    (= the general nature and character of the political situation changed)
  • "That single piece of new evidence put a completely different complexion on the murder case."
    (= it changed how the whole situation appeared and what it seemed to mean)
  • "The complexion of modern warfare has changed dramatically with the rise of drones."
    (= the overall nature and character of modern warfare has changed)
  • "The economic complexion of the region improved after several new industries were established."
    (= the general condition and character of the economy improved)
  • "The meeting took on a darker complexion when the CEO announced the layoffs."
    (= the general mood and character of the meeting became more serious and grim)

Key phrase to know: "put a different complexion on something" — this is a very common expression in English. It means that a new fact or development makes a situation look completely different from how it appeared before.

Example: "He said he had been home all night, but the security footage put a different complexion on his alibi."

Although one meaning is physical (skin) and the other is abstract (situation/character), they are connected by the same underlying idea: complexion is about the overall appearance or quality of something as you perceive it.

Just as a person's complexion is the general look and feel of their skin — telling you something about their health, their origin, their condition — the complexion of a situation is the general look and feel of it: telling you something about its nature, its seriousness, its mood, or its direction.

When used in the physical sense, you will often see it with these kinds of describing words:

  • Color-based: fair, light, pale, medium, dark, olive, golden, rosy, sallow (yellowish and unhealthy-looking)
  • Quality-based: clear, smooth, radiant, glowing, flawless, blemished, rough, uneven, dull, splotchy
  • Tone-based: warm, cool, neutral

When used in the abstract sense, you will often see:

  • Change/shift phrases: change the complexion of, alter the complexion of, put a new complexion on, put a different complexion on
  • Descriptive: political complexion, ideological complexion, moral complexion, overall complexion

UseWhat it refers to
PhysicalThe natural color, tone, clarity, and texture of a person's skin (mainly the face)
AbstractThe overall character, nature, or appearance of a situation or thing

In short: complexion is about how something looks in its totality — whether that "something" is a person's skin or a real-world situation. It captures the overall impression, not just a single detail.
3143:
Compliance means the act of doing what you are told, expected, or required to do — following a rule, a request, a standard, or a law.

When someone or something is in compliance, it means they are acting in line with what has been asked or required of them. When someone is out of compliance, they are failing to meet those requirements.

Think of it this way: someone in authority (a government, a company, a doctor, a parent) sets a rule or a standard. Compliance is what happens when the person or organization on the receiving end actually follows it.

Simple example:
A city says all restaurants must wash their hands before handling food. A restaurant that actually does this is in compliance. One that doesn't is not in compliance (or is non-compliant).

"Compliance" often carries a slight sense of obligation — you are following the rule not necessarily because you want to, but because you are required to. It's different from willingness or enthusiasm. You can comply with something you personally disagree with.

This is subtle but important. If your boss asks you to submit reports on Mondays and you do it, that's compliance — even if you'd rather not.
The Most Common Contexts Where You'll See This Word

1. Law and Government

This is the most frequent use. Governments pass laws and regulations, and businesses or individuals are expected to follow them.

"The company was fined for non-compliance with environmental regulations."
"All new buildings must be in compliance with fire safety codes."

Here, compliance is a very serious matter. Failing to comply can lead to fines, lawsuits, or even criminal charges.

2. Business and Corporate World

Large companies have entire departments called Compliance Departments. Their job is to make sure the company follows all the laws, industry rules, and internal policies that apply to it.

You'll often hear phrases like:

  • regulatory compliance — following rules set by a regulatory body (like a financial authority or health authority)
  • compliance officer — the person whose job is to ensure a company follows the rules
  • compliance audit — a check-up to see whether rules are being followed

3. Healthcare and Medicine

Doctors often use "compliance" (or its modern alternative, "adherence") to talk about whether a patient follows their prescribed treatment.

"Patient compliance with the medication schedule is essential for recovery."

If a patient is prescribed pills twice a day but keeps forgetting to take them, that's poor compliance.

4. Safety and Standards

Products, buildings, and systems often need to meet certain standards set by official bodies. If they meet those standards, they are said to be in compliance.

"This electrical wiring is not in compliance with the national safety standard."

5. Everyday and Social Contexts

Compliance can also apply in softer, less formal situations — like following instructions, agreeing to terms and conditions, or doing what someone in authority asks.

"The student's compliance with the school rules impressed the teacher."
"The website requires your compliance with its privacy policy before you can proceed."
Key Phrases and How They Work

PhraseWhat It Means
in compliancemeeting the required rules or standards
out of compliancefailing to meet them
non-compliancethe act or state of not following the rules (often carries consequences)
ensure complianceto make sure the rules are being followed
regulatory compliancefollowing rules set by an official regulating body
compliance withfollowed by whatever rule/standard/request is being referred to

(Example: "compliance with the law," "compliance with safety standards," "compliance with the doctor's orders")

It helps to distinguish it from similar words:

  • Agreement ≠ Compliance. You can comply without agreeing. A factory owner might personally think a pollution rule is too strict, but still follow it — that's compliance without agreement.
  • Obedience is very similar, but obedience is more personal and often used for people in hierarchies (a soldier obeying a commander). Compliance is broader — it applies to organizations, systems, and products too.
  • Consent is about giving permission. Compliance is about acting. You might consent to something without actually doing it, or comply with something you were never explicitly asked to consent to.

Compliance isn't always all-or-nothing. There are degrees:

  • Full compliance — everything required is being done perfectly.
  • Partial compliance — some rules are being followed, others are not.
  • Non-compliance — the rules are not being followed at all.

In legal and business settings, even partial non-compliance can trigger inspections, warnings, or penalties.

"Compliance" is one of those words that appears everywhere — in news articles, legal documents, doctor's offices, and corporate memos. Understanding it tells you:

  1. There is a rule or standard that must be followed.
  2. Someone is measuring whether that rule is being followed.
  3. There are likely consequences for not following it.

Whenever you see this word, you can ask: Who set the standard? Who is being held to it? And what happens if they don't meet it? That mental model will make the word click in every context you encounter it.
3144:
If someone or something is compliant, it means they follow the rules, meet the required standards, or do what they are asked to do — without resistance, argument, or refusal.

Think of it this way: imagine a set of rules written on a checklist. Something that is "compliant" has ticked every box on that list. A person who is "compliant" does what is expected of them.
The Two Main Ways This Word Is Used

This word is used in two broad situations:

1. When talking about a person

It describes someone who is willing to go along with what others want, what rules demand, or what authority requires. They don't push back. They follow instructions.

"The patient was compliant with the doctor's instructions and took every pill on time."

"The soldier was compliant and followed every order without question."

2. When talking about a product, system, or organization

It describes something that meets a required standard or set of regulations. This is extremely common in law, business, and technology.

"The new software is fully compliant with data privacy laws."

"The building was not compliant with fire safety regulations."

This is where the word gets more interesting and nuanced.

"Compliant" is not always purely positive. It sits on a spectrum depending on context.

When used about a thing (a product, a system, a company), it is almost always neutral or positive. It simply means the requirements are met. There is no emotional weight.

When used about a person, however, the word can carry slightly different shades:

  • Sometimes it is positive or neutral — a compliant patient takes their medicine properly; a compliant student follows classroom rules. These are good things.
  • But sometimes it carries a subtly negative or cautionary tone — a "compliant person" can suggest someone who obeys without thinking critically, who never speaks up, who is perhaps too easy to control. The word can hint at passivity, or even submission under pressure.

So context is everything. The word itself doesn't judge — but the situation around it does.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close relatives, but they are not the same:

Obedient — This word strongly suggests a hierarchy: a person in authority gives a command, and someone below follows it. A dog is obedient. A soldier is obedient. It focuses on doing what you're told by someone above you.

Submissive — This one carries a noticeably negative weight. A submissive person gives in to others' power or wishes, often because they feel they have no choice, or because they lack confidence. It implies weakness or surrender.

Cooperative — This is more positive and mutual. A cooperative person works together willingly with others toward a shared goal. It suggests teamwork, not just following orders.

Compliant — This word sits somewhere in the middle of all of these. It means following rules, standards, or requests — whether those come from a law, a doctor, a boss, or a set of technical specifications. It is more clinical and formal than the others. It doesn't require enthusiasm or genuine agreement — it just requires that the requirement is met.
A Key Insight About This Word

Here is something important to understand: compliance does not mean agreement.

A person can be compliant while completely disagreeing on the inside. A company can be compliant with a law it thinks is unfair. A patient can be compliant with a treatment they dislike. Being compliant simply means the required behavior is happening — not that the person or entity is happy about it.

This is what separates "compliant" from, say, "enthusiastic" or "supportive."

About a personWilling to follow rules, instructions, or others' wishes; not resistant or defiant
About a thing/systemMeeting required standards, rules, or regulations
Emotional weightNeutral when about things; can be neutral, mildly positive, or mildly cautionary when about people
Does NOT meanEnthusiastic, agreeable, or genuinely supportive
OppositeNon-compliant, defiant, resistant

If you want one sentence to lock this word in your memory:

"Compliant means doing what is required — following the rules, meeting the standards, or going along with what is asked — whether willingly or simply because it is expected."
3145:
To complicate something means to make it harder, messier, or more difficult to deal with — by adding something to it that wasn't there before. That something could be a new problem, a new fact, a new condition, a new emotion, or a new obstacle.

The key insight is this: complicating is always about addition. A simple, manageable thing becomes tangled, harder to understand, or harder to resolve because something new has entered the picture.
What Actually Happens When Something Gets "Complicated"

Think of a straight road. You're walking from A to B. Easy. Now imagine someone drops a wall in the middle of that road, adds three detours, and starts a thunderstorm. The destination hasn't changed. But getting there is now much harder. That's what complicating does — it doesn't erase the original goal or situation, it just layers new difficulties on top of it.

Everyday plans:
"The sudden traffic jam complicated our journey."
→ The journey was simple enough before. Traffic added a new problem and made it harder.

Health / medicine:
"His high blood pressure complicated the surgery."
→ The surgery itself was already planned. The blood pressure added extra risk, making it more difficult to perform safely.

Relationships:
"Her unexpected arrival complicated things between us."
→ There was already some situation between two people. Her arrival introduced new feelings or awkwardness that made everything harder to navigate.

Work / problem-solving:
"Don't complicate the issue — just fix the one broken part."
→ A warning not to drag in extra details or problems when you should stay focused on one simple fix.

Politics / negotiations:
"The new border dispute further complicated the peace talks."
→ The talks were already difficult. The dispute added another layer of tension and made reaching an agreement even harder.

Complicating can happen in both ways, and the word works for either.

Unintentional (nobody meant to cause difficulty — it just happened):
"Bad weather complicated the rescue mission."
→ The weather didn't choose to make things hard. It just did.

Intentional (someone chose to add difficulty):
"He deliberately complicated the negotiations by raising old arguments."
→ He made a conscious choice to introduce obstacles.

The word itself doesn't tell you which one it is — you understand that from the context.

This is one of the most common ways you'll see this word used. The structure is:

[Something] was complicated by [the new factor].

  • "The mission was complicated by poor visibility."
  • "The recovery was complicated by a second infection."
  • "Their relationship was complicated by distance."

Here, the thing being complicated (the mission, the recovery, the relationship) is receiving the difficulty. The thing after "by" is what introduced that difficulty. This structure is everywhere in news, formal writing, and everyday conversation.

These combinations appear so often that they're almost fixed expressions:

  • Complicate matters — the most common. "This new development complicates matters."
  • Complicate things — same idea, more informal. "Don't complicate things."
  • Complicate the situation — "His reaction only complicated the situation."
  • Complicate someone's life — "The unexpected debt complicated her life enormously."
  • Further complicate — used when something was already complex and is now even more so. "The new law further complicates an already confusing process."
  • Unnecessarily complicate — adds the judgment that the added complexity wasn't needed. "You're unnecessarily complicating a simple task."
  • Only complicates — suggests the addition makes things worse without any benefit. "Arguing about blame only complicates the problem."

In everyday conversation, when someone says "You're complicating this" or "Don't complicate it," there's often a tone of mild frustration. The speaker is saying: this was manageable, and you're making it harder than it needs to be. It implies the extra complexity is unnecessary or counterproductive.

This use is very natural in spoken English:

  • "Stop complicating everything."
  • "I don't want to complicate things between us."
  • "Let's not complicate this."

In these cases, the speaker is often also asking the other person to step back, simplify their thinking, and not bring in extra emotional weight or extra conditions.

It's worth being clear about what this word does not mean, so you don't mix it up with similar words:

  • It does not mean to destroy or ruin something. A complicated plan is still a plan — just harder to execute.
  • It does not simply mean "to confuse someone." Confusion may result from complicating, but the word is about the situation, not just about someone's state of mind.
  • It does not mean to make something impossible — only harder or messier.
  • It is not the same as "to create from scratch." You complicate something that already exists.

To complicate something is to make it harder, more tangled, or more difficult to handle — by introducing a new factor, problem, or layer that was not there before. The original situation remains, but it is now heavier, messier, or harder to resolve because of what has been added to it.

That's the full picture of "complicate" as a verb — its meaning, mechanics, uses across contexts, passive form, common phrases, social tone, and boundaries. You now have everything you need.
3146:
Something is complicated when it has many parts, steps, layers, or moving pieces — and because of that, it becomes hard to understand, explain, solve, or deal with.

Think of it this way: the opposite of complicated is simple. A simple thing has few parts and is easy to grasp. A complicated thing has many parts that interact with each other in messy or tangled ways, making it hard to get a clear picture of the whole thing.
The two main ways it's used

1. Something is complicated because it has too many parts or steps

This is the most literal use. It describes things in the real world — machines, instructions, processes, systems — that are difficult to understand or work through because of their sheer intricacy.

"The engine is very complicated — it has hundreds of tiny components all working together."

"The process of applying for a visa is incredibly complicated. There are twenty forms, each with dozens of questions."

"She tried to follow the recipe, but it was too complicated — it required special tools and fifteen ingredients she'd never heard of."

Here, "complicated" is pointing at objective difficulty. The thing genuinely has a lot going on.

2. Something is complicated because of tangled emotions, relationships, or situations

This is a softer, more emotional use. When people, feelings, or circumstances are complicated, it means they're hard to sort through — not because of physical parts, but because of competing feelings, unclear boundaries, conflicting interests, or layers of history.

"Their friendship is complicated. They used to be in a relationship, then had a falling out, and now they're trying to be friends again."

"My feelings about my hometown are complicated — I love it, but it also holds painful memories."

"It's a complicated situation. If I take the promotion, I'll have to move cities, which would mean leaving my family behind."

The famous phrase "It's complicated" — which many people say when asked about a relationship — captures this perfectly. It's a shorthand way of saying: "The situation has so many layers and conflicting feelings that I can't explain it simply."
What "complicated" implies beyond its literal meaning

When someone calls something complicated, there's usually a subtle undertone of frustration, reluctance, or weariness. It often implies the speaker wishes things were simpler, or that the difficulty feels excessive — perhaps even unnecessary.

Compare:

  • "This is a simple task." → Easy, no problem.
  • "This is a complicated task." → This is more difficult than I'd like; there's a lot to deal with.

In other words, "complicated" doesn't just describe a fact — it often carries a slight emotional charge. It signals that someone is finding something burdensome or tiring to navigate.
How "complicated" compares to words that seem similar

Complicated vs. difficult

"Difficult" is about how much effort or ability something requires. "Complicated" is about how many parts or layers something has.

Something can be difficult without being complicated. Lifting a 200-kg boulder is difficult (it requires enormous strength) but it's not complicated (there's nothing intricate about it — you just lift it).

Something can be complicated without feeling difficult, especially if you are an expert. A seasoned surgeon might say a procedure is complicated (it has many precise steps) but not difficult for them personally.

Often the two words go together — complicated things tend to become difficult because of their many parts — but they're not the same idea.

Complicated vs. complex

In everyday speech, people use these almost interchangeably, and that's perfectly fine. But if you want the precise distinction:

  • Complex describes something that has many interconnected parts by nature — a living ecosystem, the human brain, a city's social fabric. The intricacy is inherent and often even beautiful or impressive. "Complex" doesn't carry a negative feeling.
  • Complicated more often implies that the difficulty is somewhat excessive, inconvenient, or at least unwelcome — even if it's unavoidable. It can suggest that things could be simplified, or that the difficulty is a nuisance.

A spider's web is complex — elegantly intricate by nature.
A tax return form is complicated — needlessly difficult to fill out.

Again, in normal conversation, most people don't make this distinction and use both words freely.

Complicated vs. confusing

"Confusing" focuses on your reaction — it means something causes you to be unclear or mixed up. "Complicated" focuses on the thing itself — it means the thing has many parts or layers.

A badly written explanation can be confusing without the underlying idea being complicated. A quantum physics equation can be complicated but, to an expert, not at all confusing.
How it behaves as a word (without getting technical)

"Complicated" comes in degrees. Things aren't just complicated or not complicated — they can be:

  • a little complicated
  • quite complicated
  • very complicated
  • incredibly complicated
  • needlessly complicated (meaning: it's more complicated than it needs to be)

You'll also often see it paired with words like:

  • a complicated situation
  • a complicated relationship
  • a complicated process
  • a complicated question
  • a complicated history (meaning a past full of difficult or tangled events)
  • things got complicated (meaning: the situation became harder to deal with)

If you had to remember just one thing: complicated = made of many tangled or interlocking parts that make understanding or handling it hard.

Whether it's a machine, a problem, a feeling, or a human relationship — if it's hard to sort through because of its many moving pieces, it's complicated.

And when someone says "it's complicated," they're usually also hinting: "I wish it weren't."
3147:
When someone is complicit in something wrong or harmful, they share in the moral responsibility for it — even though they may not have done the harmful thing directly.

Complicit sits in the space between "I did it" and "I had nothing to do with it." It captures a middle ground: you were connected to a wrongdoing — through your actions, your knowledge, or even your silence — in a way that made it possible, easier, or able to continue.
You don't have to be the main actor

This is the heart of the word. Complicit always implies that someone else is committing the main wrongful act — but you are meaningfully tied to it. You might be the person who helped plan it, the person who supplied the tools or money that made it possible, the person who knew it was happening and said nothing, or the person who helped cover it up afterward. All of these people can be called complicit.

One of the most important applications of the word — and one that surprises many learners — is that complicit can describe pure inaction. If you knew something wrong was happening, had a real opportunity to speak up or stop it, and chose to say nothing, your silence can make you complicit. The logic is that silence, in that situation, is not neutrality. The wrongdoing continued at least in part because you allowed it to.

This is why phrases like "your silence makes you complicit" appear so often in moral and political discussions. Not acting, when you reasonably could have and should have, is itself treated as a form of participation.

Not all complicit people are equally responsible. Complicity exists on a spectrum. A person who actively planned a fraud scheme is far more complicit than a colleague who simply stayed quiet after accidentally learning about it. A person who supplied money knowing it would fund something harmful is more complicit than someone who unknowingly signed a misleading document. The word applies across this entire range — but the degree of moral blame it carries shifts accordingly.

A bank manager notices a client making thousands of suspicious transactions that look like money laundering. He stays quiet because the client brings in a lot of revenue. That manager is complicit in the money laundering.

A group of students watches a classmate being bullied every day. They don't bully the classmate themselves, but they laugh along, never intervene, and never tell a teacher. They are complicit in the bullying.

Senior executives at a company discover that their factory has been dumping toxic waste into a river. They stay quiet because cleanup would cost millions. They are complicit in the environmental damage.

A journalist publishes a story she knows contains false accusations about someone, simply because it will get clicks. She is complicit in the reputational harm caused to that person.

In every example, the person did not commit the core wrong directly — but their knowledge, inaction, or involvement tied them to it morally.

Complicit is not the same as being the primary wrongdoer. A person who committed a crime is guilty of that crime. A person who knew about it, stayed silent, and helped cover it up is complicit — different in degree, but still morally accountable.

It also does not apply just from being nearby or vaguely aware. There has to be meaningful involvement, or a meaningful failure to act when action was genuinely possible and reasonably expected of someone in that position.

It also doesn't apply if you were truly deceived. If you participated in something wrong but were genuinely misled and had no real way of knowing, you're generally not considered complicit. Knowledge — or the reasonable expectation that you should have had knowledge — is almost always central to the accusation.
The moral weight of the word

Complicit is a serious, weighty word. When you call someone complicit, you are making a real moral accusation. It implies shared guilt — not full, primary guilt, but genuine shared guilt. It says: you had the opportunity to act differently, and you didn't, and because of that, you bear a portion of responsibility for what happened.

This is why the word is so commonly used in serious contexts — crime, political corruption, corporate misconduct, social injustice, institutional abuse. It cuts through the defense of "I didn't actually do anything." Its reply to that defense is pointed: in this case, not doing anything was itself the wrong.

Complicit is almost always used after a linking verb — you say "she is complicit," "they were found complicit," "he became complicit" — rather than directly before a noun. Saying "the complicit employees" is technically possible but sounds unusual; the more natural construction is "the employees who were complicit."

The word is nearly always followed by "in" and then the wrongdoing: complicit in the fraud, complicit in the cover-up, complicit in the abuse, complicit in the deception.
A few more usage examples to cement it

"By staying silent for years, the witnesses became complicit in the injustice." "She refused to sign the document because doing so would make her complicit." "The entire department was accused of being complicit in the misconduct." "He didn't want to be complicit in something he knew was wrong, so he resigned."

In summary: complicit means you share moral responsibility for a wrong — not necessarily because you committed it, but because you were knowingly involved, helped enable it, or failed to stop it when you reasonably could have. The word holds people accountable for the space between innocence and direct guilt, and it treats silence and inaction as meaningful choices, not safe ones.
3148:
Complicity means being involved in a wrongdoing that someone else committed — not necessarily as the main person who did it, but in a way that helped it happen, allowed it to happen, or made it easier for it to happen. It is the state of sharing responsibility for something harmful or wrong.

The essential idea is this: you don't have to be the one who "did the thing" to be responsible for it. If your involvement — in any form — contributed to a wrong act, you have complicity in it.

Think of complicity as a bridge between you and a wrongdoing. Even if you are not standing at the center of that wrongdoing, your actions (or your deliberate inaction) built a path to it.

Here is a simple, concrete example. Suppose your friend plans to steal money from a shop, and you agree to stand outside and whistle if you see a security guard coming. You never touched the money. You didn't walk into the shop. But your role as a lookout made the theft possible. You have complicity in the theft. The law would call you an accomplice — the person in whom complicity lives.

Now here is where the word gets deeper and more interesting.

One of the most powerful and debated aspects of complicity is that you can be complicit without doing anything at all. If you know about a wrongdoing and stay silent — when you had the ability and the opportunity to speak up or stop it — many people (and many legal systems) consider you complicit.

This is the origin of the widely-used phrase "silence is complicity." If a group of your colleagues is being dishonest to customers, and you know about it, and you say nothing and do nothing, you are allowing it to continue. Your silence becomes part of the machinery that keeps the wrong act running. You share in its responsibility.

This passive form of complicity is often harder for people to accept, because it feels unfair — "I didn't do anything!" But that is precisely the point: you didn't do anything, and something wrong happened because of it.

Complicity almost always requires some level of awareness. This is what separates complicity from innocent, accidental involvement.

If someone deceives you into helping them do something wrong — say, a friend asks you to deliver a package "as a favor," and it turns out to contain stolen goods, and you genuinely had no idea — that is generally not complicity. You didn't know. You couldn't have known.

But if you had a nagging suspicion and chose to ignore it, or if the signs were clear and you looked the other way anyway, that awareness (or deliberate avoidance of awareness) is enough to make you complicit. The law and moral philosophy both take a hard look at what you knew or should reasonably have known.

Complicity exists on a spectrum. At one end, you have someone who helped plan a crime from the very beginning — deeply, actively complicit. At the other end, you have someone who simply knew about a minor wrong and stayed quiet — a much lighter form of complicity, but complicity nonetheless.

Some common forms:

Active complicity — You played a direct role. You provided tools, money, information, cover, or physical help. You were "in on it."

Passive complicity — You knew and said nothing. You witnessed a wrong and chose not to intervene, report, or resist it, even though you could have.

Institutional or systemic complicity — This is a broader, social concept. When people benefit from an unjust system and do nothing to challenge it, they can be said to share in its complicity. This is common language in conversations about structural inequality, political corruption, or institutional misconduct.

It helps to know where the edges of the word are.

Complicity is not the same as being the main wrongdoer. The person who commits the crime is the criminal. The person who drove the getaway car, helped plan it, or covered for the criminal has complicity — but they are not the same as the one who pulled the trigger, so to speak.

Complicity is not mere association. Simply being friends with, related to, or in the same room as someone who does something wrong does not make you complicit. Complicity requires that your role — however small — connected to the wrongdoing in some meaningful way.

Complicity is not accidental. If you genuinely, reasonably had no idea that something wrong was happening, that is not complicity. The awareness piece is essential.
The Moral Weight of the Word

This is important to understand: complicity is not a neutral word. It carries moral and ethical weight. When someone says you have complicity in something, they are not merely describing where you were standing. They are making a claim about your responsibility — that some part of what went wrong belongs to you.

This is why the word frequently appears in serious conversations — courtrooms, political debates, ethical philosophy, social justice movements. It is the language of accountability. It asks: who else, beyond the obvious wrongdoer, bears responsibility here?
How It Is Used in a Sentence

A few natural examples to cement your understanding:

"His complicity in the cover-up was proven when investigators found his emails."
Here, he actively helped hide the truth. His involvement made the cover-up work.

"By remaining silent, the board members showed their complicity in the fraud."
They didn't commit fraud, but their silence protected those who did.

"She refused to be drawn into complicity with a system she believed was unjust."
She was being asked — perhaps pressured — to participate in or support something wrong, and she resisted.

If you ever need to remember what complicity means in its simplest form, hold onto this:

Complicity is the shared responsibility for a wrong — not because you did it yourself, but because you were part of it in some way, whether through action, assistance, or knowing silence.
3149:
A compliment is something kind and positive that you say to someone — specifically to express praise, admiration, or approval of them, their qualities, their actions, or something they own.

When you give someone a compliment, you are verbally recognizing something good about them. The purpose is to make that person feel seen, appreciated, or good about themselves.

"You have a beautiful smile."
"You did a fantastic job on that presentation."
"Your cooking is extraordinary."

All three of these are compliments.
What a Compliment Is Really About

A compliment is always directed at someone. It's not just a general positive statement — it's a positive statement about a specific person (or something closely connected to them), shared with that person.

If you tell your friend, "I think Ravi is very intelligent," that's not a compliment to Ravi — Ravi isn't there. But if you say directly to Ravi, "You are very intelligent," that is a compliment.

The key ingredients:

  • It is positive (praise, admiration, appreciation)
  • It is addressed to or about the person who receives it
  • It is meant to please or honor the receiver

Compliments can be about almost anything connected to a person:

  • Appearance — "You look great today."
  • Talent or skill — "You're an incredible writer."
  • Character or personality — "You are one of the most patient people I know."
  • Work or achievement — "This report you wrote is outstanding."
  • Taste or possessions — "Your apartment is so well-decorated."
  • Actions or behavior — "The way you handled that situation was really mature."

Not all compliments are equally genuine.

A sincere compliment comes from honest observation and genuine feeling. The person actually believes what they are saying. These tend to feel meaningful and memorable to the receiver.

An empty or hollow compliment is said without real meaning — perhaps to please someone, to flatter them for personal gain, or simply out of habit. "Oh, everything you do is absolutely perfect!" said casually to everyone is more flattery than a true compliment. While it may still please the listener, it carries less weight.

This distinction matters because in serious contexts — at work, in a relationship, in writing — a sincere compliment holds real value, while hollow flattery can eventually erode trust.

Pay someone a compliment
This is the standard way to say you gave someone a compliment. The word "pay" here doesn't mean money — it's an older usage meaning "to offer" or "to give."
"She paid him a compliment on his leadership skills."

Return the compliment
When someone compliments you and you compliment them back, you are returning the compliment.
"He said I played well, and I returned the compliment."

Fish for compliments
When someone behaves in a way that is clearly designed to get others to praise them — usually by saying something self-critical so others rush to reassure them.
"She kept saying her dress looked terrible, but she was just fishing for compliments."

Take something as a compliment
To interpret something (even something not obviously nice) as a positive thing being said about you.
"He said I argue like a lawyer — I'll take that as a compliment."

When "compliment" is used in the plural — compliments — it often takes on a slightly different, more formal flavor, especially in set phrases:

"Compliments of [someone]"
This means something is being given or offered as a gesture of goodwill or generosity, free of charge, as a kind gift from the named person or organization.
"The dessert is compliments of the chef." (= The chef is sending it to you as a gift, no charge.)
"With compliments from the management."

"Compliments of the season"
A traditional, somewhat formal expression used especially around holidays (like Christmas or New Year) to wish someone well. It's like saying "best wishes during this festive time."

"Give my compliments to..."
Used to send your praise or warm regards to someone who is not present.
"Please give my compliments to the cook — the food was excellent."
A Very Common Mistake: Compliment vs. Complement

These two words sound identical when spoken, so they are confused very often — even by native speakers.

Compliment (with an i) — what we've been discussing. Something kind said to honor or praise someone.
"That was a wonderful compliment."

Complement (with an e) — means something that completes, pairs perfectly with, or goes well with something else. It has nothing to do with praise.
"The wine is a perfect complement to the meal." (= The wine and the meal go together beautifully.)

A simple memory trick: compliment with an i → think of "I" → it's about honoring a person. Complement with an e → think of "complete" → it's about things completing each other.
The Social Role of a Compliment

Compliments are a small but important part of how humans connect. A well-placed, sincere compliment can:

  • Strengthen a friendship or relationship
  • Boost someone's confidence at a crucial moment
  • Create goodwill between strangers or colleagues
  • Make someone feel noticed and valued

Because compliments have this social power, they are also sometimes used strategically — to win someone's favor or soften them before making a request. This isn't necessarily dishonest, but it's worth being aware of.

The difference between a compliment that feels wonderful and one that feels suspicious often lies in specificity and timing. A compliment that names something particular and real ("The way you explained that complex topic so simply was impressive") feels more genuine than a vague, sweeping one ("You're just amazing at everything").
A compliment is a verbal expression of praise or admiration directed at a person — said to acknowledge something good about them and to make them feel appreciated.
